Kernel-SDF: An Open-Source Library for Real-Time Signed
Distance Function Estimation using Kernel Regression
Zhirui Dai1,*Tianxing Fan1,*Mani Amani1Jaemin Seo2
Ki Myung Brian Lee1Hyondong Oh2Nikolay Atanasov1
Abstract—Accurate and efficient environment representation
is crucial for robotic applications such as motion planning,
manipulation, and navigation. Signed distance functions (SDFs)
have emerged as a powerful representation for encoding distance
to obstacle boundaries, enabling efficient collision-checking and
trajectory optimization techniques. However, existing SDF re-
construction methods have limitations when it comes to large-
scale uncertainty-aware SDF estimation from streaming sensor
data. Voxel-based approaches are limited by fixed resolution and
lack uncertainty quantification, neural network methods require
significant training time, while Gaussian process (GP) methods
struggle with scalability, sign estimation, and uncertainty calibra-
tion. In this letter, we develop an open-source library, Kernel-
SDF, which uses kernel regression to learn SDF with calibrated
uncertainty quantification in real-time. Our approach consists of
a front-end that learns a continuous occupancy field via kernel
regression, and a back-end that estimates accurate SDF via GP
regression using samples from the front-end surface boundaries.
Kernel-SDF provides accurate SDF, SDF gradient, SDF uncer-
tainty, and mesh construction in real-time. Evaluation results
show that Kernel-SDF achieves superior accuracy compared
to existing methods, while maintaining real-time performance,
making it suitable for various robotics applications requiring
reliable uncertainty-aware geometric information.
I. INTRODUCTION
Geometric environment representations play a key role
for many robot autonomy capabilities, including mapping,
localization, motion planning, manipulation, and navigation.
An ideal representation should meet several requirements:
1) accuracy to reflect the environment structure, 2) compu-
tational efficiency to allow real-time processing of streaming
sensor information, 3) scalability to capture large environ-
ments, 4) robustness to noise, 5) uncertainty quantification to
support risk-aware decision making, 6) differentiability to sup-
port gradient-based optimization, 7) adaptability to dynamic
environments, and 8) compatibility with different sensors.
Various effective representations have been proposed in the
literature: occupancy data structures [1], point clouds [2]–[4],
meshes [5], [6], and implicit functions such as signed distance
function (SDF) [7]–[24] and neural radiance field (NeRF)
[25]. Among these, SDFs have attracted attention due to their
ability to provide the distance to the nearest obstacles, which
is useful for mapping [7], [24] and motion planning [26], [27].

Furthermore, differentiable SDF methods can be used to define
safety constraints in navigation [28] and manipulation [29].
Various methods have been proposed to learn SDFs from
range sensors, such as LiDAR or depth camera. V oxel-based
methods [7], [8], [10], [15] often focus only on truncated SDF
(TSDF) estimation but some [8], [10], [30], [31] are able
to reconstruct non-truncated (Euclidean) SDF on a discrete
grid. These methods maintain a dense discrete approximation
of (T)SDF with fixed resolution, which leads to a trade-off
between accuracy and computational efficiency and prevents
differentiability. In contrast, neural network methods [9], [17]–
[19], [21], [24] learn SDF as a continuous function, avoiding
an explicit grid representation and providing accurate and
differentiable approximations. However, these methods are not
suitable for online learning due to the significant training time
needed to converge to a good SDF estimate.
Gaussian process (GP) methods [11], [12], [22], [23] are
non-parametric and capable of estimating accurate Euclidean
SDF. However, existing GP methods scale poorly with in-
creasing environment sizes, lack robust sign estimation, and
report variance estimates that are inconsistent with actual
SDF prediction errors. To enable scalability, octree [12] and
OpenVDB [23] data structures are used to split the training
data into smaller chunks for training multiple GPs. To provide
consistent sign and variance estimates, GMMGP [22] uses an
SDF prior from a hierarchical Gaussian mixture model but this
prior provides increasingly larger errors as the query position
moves further away from the surface.
In this letter, we develop an open-source library, Kernel-
SDF, for SDF estimation, meeting the aforementioned require-
ments for an effective geometric representation and addressing
the limitations of the existing GP methods. To achieve this,
Kernel-SDF maintains an octree data structure to split the
estimation process into smaller areas, estimates the occupan-
cy/sign in each octant using a Bayesian Hilbert map (BHM)arXiv:2603.29227v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

[32], and reconstructs SDF via GP regression from the BHM
surface samples. Thus, the library is organized as a surface
estimation front-end, performing BHM occupancy estimation,
and an SDF prediction back-end, preforming GP regression.
The front-end learns a continuous occupancy field for robust
sign estimation and provides surface point samples via the
marching cubes algorithm [33]. The back-end uses the surface
point samples to train SDF GPs in each octant with integrated
uncertainty quantification. We introduce several optimizations
to ensure real-time performance and map consistency: spa-
tial partitioning and priority-queue-based updates for efficient
computation and BHM weight synchronization to maintain
consistency across neighboring local maps.
Kernel-SDF provides accurate SDF, SDF gradient, SDF
uncertainty, and mesh construction in real time (see Fig. 1).
In summary, our contributions include:
1) an open-source C++ implementation1for 2D/3D SDF
learning, featuring Python and ROS1/ROS2 interfaces
with extensive real-time testing;
2) a highly-optimized kernel regression method for real-
time SDF learning via two components: BHM front-end
for continuous occupancy learning and uncertainty-aware
surface extraction, and GP back-end for SDF and SDF
gradient prediction with uncertainty;
3) five strategies to achieve efficiency and robustness:
octree-based partitioning for local region learning, op-
timized data processing for rapid training set generation,
weight synchronization for map consistency, adaptive
scaling for GP stability, and priority-queue-based updates
to balance accuracy with responsiveness.
II. RELATEDWORK
SDF learning methods can be categorized as voxel-based,
neural-net-based, and Gaussian-process-based.
A. Voxel Methods
Many methods have been proposed to learn SDF using a
grid [34]. KinectFusion [7] pioneered real-time 3D reconstruc-
tion using depth sensors based on projective TSDF. Follow-up
works, such as V oxblox [8], extended this to Euclidean SDF
by breadth-first-search (BFS) integration from the occupied
voxels. However, projective TSDF estimates the true SDF as
distance along camera rays, which is inaccurate, and BFS
integration introduces additional errors. FIESTA [10] inte-
grates SDF estimation with an occupancy map, replacing the
BFS-based distance with the distance to the nearest occupied
voxel. V oxField [16] formulates non-projective TSDF, though
its accuracy relies on the quality of estimated surface nor-
mals and SDF gradients. A common limitation among these
methods is the use of fixed-resolution grids, which restricts
scalability in larger environments. VDBblox [30] and nvblox
[31] address scalability by using OpenVDB [35] or GPU-based
voxel hashing. However, voxel-based methods lack uncertainty
quantification and are usually not differentiable.

Neural network methods offer differentiability by design
and can achieve highly accurate SDF reconstruction, as shown
by DeepSDF [9]. DeepSDF uses an MLP with latent features
to learn SDF of objects. NeuS [13] and NeuS2 [18] combine
SDF with neural radiance fields (NeRF) [25] to jointly learn
SDF and rendering. PIN-SLAM [21] and MISO [24] imple-
ment simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) based
on an SDF map encoded using neural features. H 2-Mapping
[19] uses a voxel SDF prior and a neural TSDF residual, which
are co-optimized with volumetric rendering. However, most
neural network methods do not meet real-time requirements
for operating in novel environments due to their significant
training time. Although some works, like H 2-Mapping [19]
and PIN-SLAM [21], achieve neural SDF learning online, they
sacrifice the SDF accuracy very much.
C. Gaussian Process Methods
GP methods are suitable for online SDF learning but face
challenges related to the high computational cost of kernel
matrix inversion as the environment scale increases. To mit-
igate this, GPIS [11] employs octree-based data partitioning
and trains multiple GPs for each local partition. However, its
SDF estimates quickly revert to the zero-mean prior away from
the surface. Log-GPIS [12] observes an important connection
between the heat kernel and the unsigned distance function,
and formulates unsigned distance field GP regression in log
space. However, the log transformation does not consider
sign information and distorts variance estimation, causing
uncertainty to explode far from the surface. Furthermore,
the surface estimation in Log-GPIS is sensitive to sensor
noise and dynamic environmental changes. VDB-GPDF [23]
improves surface estimation through OpenVDB TSDF fusion
but does not provide sign estimates or reliable uncertainty
quantification. To overcome these limitations, we introduce
a continuous occupancy field front-end in Kernel-SDF based
on BHM [32], [36], which provides robust sign prediction
and accurate surface estimation, even in dynamic or noisy
environments. Our GP back-end, then, learns SDF from the
surface samples and formulates an uncertainty estimate that
respects the SDF errors to deliver precise SDF and gradient
predictions with reliable uncertainty quantification.

IV. KERNEL-SDF
Our approach, Kernel-SDF, consists of a surface estimation
front-end using BHM [32] (Sec. IV-A) and an SDF prediction
back-end using GP regression [37] (Sec. IV-B). Both BHMs
and GPs are kernel regression methods that support continu-
ous representations with uncertainty quantification. However,
directly applying kernel regression over the entire environment
is computationally expensive and impractical for real-time
applications. Kernel-SDF addresses this by partitioning the
environment into multiple local regions, defined by an octree
data structure, and applying kernel regression within each
region with additional optimization techniques. Fig. 2 provides
an overview of Kernel-SDF.

C. Priority Queue Based Update
Beyond the core BHM and GP optimizations, we also
use priority-queue-based update to improve the efficiency.
Frequent sensor measurements make running surface extrac-
tion, updating GP training data buffer, and GP training after
every BHM update computationally wasteful. To optimize
performance, we delay these processes until necessary us-
ing a three-queue priority system shown in Fig. 2. To stay
responsive, frequently queried GPs get higher priority for
data buffer updates and retraining. Besides, BHMs with the
oldest marching request timestamps are prioritized to process
regions that are likely to remain stable. This strategy ensures
computational resources are focused on high-demand areas
while maintaining overall map correctness.
V. EXPERIMENTS
We compare Kernel-SDF to four baselines: V oxblox [8],
FIESTA [10], iSDF [17], and VDB-GPDF [23] on the Replica
[39], Cow and Lady [8] and Newer College [40] datasets.
For Replica, we simulate depth noise using an axial model
withσ= 0.0025z2[41]. We first analyze reconstruction
quality (Sec. V-A) and SDF accuracy (Sec. V-B), followed
by an assessment of computational efficiency (Sec. V-C). We,
then, verify the consistency between estimated SDF variance
and actual error (Sec. V-D) and study the impact of sensor
noise (Sec. V-E). Finally, we demonstrate real-world robot
navigation using Kernel-SDF (Sec. V-F).

A. Reconstruction Accuracy
Visual comparisons in Figs. 5, 6, and 7 demonstrate that
Kernel-SDF produces high-quality meshes that closely resem-
ble the ground truth models. On the low-noise Replica dataset,
V oxblox [8], FIESTA [10] and VDB-GPDF [23] exhibit voxel-
induced block artifacts, while iSDF [17] yields over-smoothed
surfaces. These baselines perform worse in real-world datasets
(Cow and Lady, Newer College), where sensor noise leads
to incomplete or distorted meshes. Specifically, the discrete
grids used in FIESTA, V oxblox and VDB-GPDF struggle with
fine details and completeness, while iSDF consistently lacks
geometric details.
Quantitative results in Table II confirm that our method
achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance across
nearly all metrics and datasets. By effectively mitigating sensor
noise while preserving fine geometric details, Kernel-SDF
consistently outperforms the baselines.

F . Autonomous Robot Navigation Case Study
Real-time, uncertainty-quantified SDF mapping is essential
for safe robot navigation. We demonstrate this by constructing
a safe navigation corridor from a chain of overlapping bub-
bles, by planning in the SDF map using the sampling-based
approach proposed in [26]. The planner constructs a rapidly
exploring random tree from sampled positions in free space
with associated safe bubbles. The radii are specified by the

SDF values minus a safety margin, which can be scaled by the
estimated SDF uncertainty. As shown in Fig. 10, the planner
recovers a connected chain of SDF bubbles spanning the start
and goal positions, ensuring the path remains strictly within
the mapped free space. This case study validates the utility of
Kernel-SDF in providing the accurate distance and uncertainty
information required for risk-aware motion planning.
VI. CONCLUSION
We presented Kernel-SDF, a real-time kernel regression
framework for differentiable SDF learning with uncertainty
quantification. By coupling BHMs for robust surface estima-
tion with GPs for distance prediction, our method achieves
superior reconstruction accuracy and efficiency. The hierar-
chical tree structure ensures scalability for large-scale en-
vironments, while our softmin-based uncertainty quantifi-
cation enables risk-aware decision-making for downstream
robotic tasks. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real-
world datasets demonstrate that Kernel-SDF outperforms state-
of-the-art baselines in both quality and speed. Furthermore,
our BHM-based front-end effectively mitigates sensor noise
and adapts to dynamic environments, providing a robust and
practical solution for real-time robotic applications.

In Kernel-SDF, several operations take significant time,
including BHM EM update, BHM marching, GP training

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces Kernel-SDF, an open-source library designed for real-time Signed Distance Function (SDF) estimation using kernel regression. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Existing methods for SDF reconstruction from streaming sensor data struggle with large-scale environments, uncertainty quantification, training time, scalability, and accurate sign estimation.
*   **Solution:** Kernel-SDF utilizes a two-component approach:
    *   **Front-end:** A kernel regression-based component learns a continuous occupancy field, providing robust sign estimation and surface point samples.
    *   **Back-end:** A Gaussian Process (GP) regression component estimates accurate SDF and its gradient from the surface samples, with calibrated uncertainty quantification.
*   **Key Features:** Kernel-SDF provides accurate SDF, SDF gradient, SDF uncertainty, and mesh construction in real-time.
*   **Contributions:**
    *   An open-source C++ implementation with Python and ROS interfaces.
    *   A highly optimized kernel regression method combining a Bayesian Hilbert Map (BHM) front-end and a GP back-end.
    *   Five strategies for efficiency and robustness: octree-based partitioning, optimized data processing, weight synchronization, adaptive scaling, and priority-queue-based updates.
*   **Comparison to Existing Methods:** The document highlights the limitations of voxel-based (fixed resolution, no uncertainty), neural network-based (long training times), and existing Gaussian Process-based methods (scalability, sign estimation, uncertainty calibration) and positions Kernel-SDF as a superior alternative.
*   **Requirements for Geometric Representation:** The introduction outlines desirable characteristics for robot environment representations, including accuracy, computational efficiency, scalability, robustness, uncertainty quantification, differentiability, adaptability, and sensor compatibility, which Kernel-SDF aims to fulfill.
